name: The Brochure vs. Our Actual Tuesday
why_it_works: Polished professional brands feel distant. Laughing at your own stock-photo image first makes you look confident and real, and the small, harmless chaos of a normal Tuesday is relatable. Then the one thing that never slips lands as sincere, because you already proved you won't oversell.

hook.pattern: Split the screen: what people imagine your kind of business looks like vs. a real, slightly chaotic day.
examples: The brochure {{business_type}} vs. our actual Tuesday.

variables.name: business_type
variables.description: The kind of business, as people would say it

variables.name: brochure_cliche
variables.description: The glossy stock-photo cliche of the industry, starting with a capital letter (10 words or fewer, spoken)
variables.example: Five people laughing at one salad in a glass boardroom

variables.name: tuesday_reality_1
variables.description: A harmless, self-deprecating real detail, starting with a capital letter (11 words or fewer, spoken)
variables.example: The printer has jammed. The printer has a name. It's Gerald.

variables.name: tuesday_reality_2
variables.description: A second real detail, slightly bigger, starting with a capital letter (11 words or fewer, spoken)
variables.example: A 20-minute team debate about which lunch place is 'close'

variables.name: callback_tag
variables.description: A short callback to the first Tuesday detail (4 words or fewer)

variables.name: the_standard
variables.description: The one thing that never slips, stated as a process, not a result, starting with a capital letter (9 words or fewer, spoken)
variables.example: Every client call returned the same business day

variables.name: standard_proof
variables.description: A real, checkable number from your own records that backs the standard (12 words or fewer); never invent it
variables.example: Last month: 214 client calls, 214 returned the same day.

variables.name: offer
variables.description: What the viewer gets for acting

variables.name: disclosure
variables.description: Required fine print for the client's niche, copied from the matching pack in compliance/packs.json
variables.example: Attorney advertising. Past results do not guarantee a similar outcome.

visual.prompt: Vertical 9:16 split screen: top half a glossy, overlit stock-photo style office with posed smiling professionals, bottom half the real {{brand}} office, lived-in, warm natural light, coffee cups on desks
Vertical overly perfect stock-style photo of {{brochure_cliche}}, harsh bright white light, impossibly clean glass office, exaggerated posed smiles, slightly too saturated
Vertical candid documentary photo inside {{brand}} showing {{tuesday_reality_1}}, real staff in everyday work clothes, natural window light, slightly messy desk, warm and human
Vertical handheld clip, a small group of {{brand}} staff in a lively, friendly debate around a desk about {{tuesday_reality_2}}, gestures, laughter, natural office light, documentary feel

beats.purpose: turn: the thing that never changes
beats.voiceover: What doesn't change, Tuesday or not: {{the_standard}}.

visual.prompt: Vertical calm medium shot of a team member from {{brand}} focused at their desk with a client file or phone, quiet focused light, the chaos softly blurred behind them, sincere mood

cta: Book {{offer}} with {{brand}}. Real people, real Tuesdays.

craft.technique: Self-deprecating expectation vs. reality with a sincere turn
craft.notes: Setup: the brochure cliche, shot deliberately too glossy so the audience laughs at the stock-photo look, not at anyone. Escalation: two Tuesday details that climb from small (a printer with a name) to bigger (a whole team debate), each one at the brand's own expense. Turn: the music drops out and the tone goes sincere for the one standard that never slips. Tag: a callback to the first reality detail (the callback_tag, e.g. 'Gerald is still jammed.') so the ad ends on a laugh, not a lecture. Timing: hard cut from brochure to Tuesday on the downbeat; leave a full beat of quiet before the turn line, and land the tag within half a second after it so the sincerity doesn't overstay.

do_not: Make the 'reality' look incompetent with client work, files or money; the chaos is only about printers, lunch and office life
Mock a competitor's office or real stock photos from a named source
State the standard as an outcome (wins, returns, results); keep it a process
Show real client names, files or screens in any frame
compliance: Law firms: no outcome or settlement claims; the standard must be about service (response time), not results; label as attorney advertising where your state bar requires; no actors posing as clients without a disclaimer
Financial advisors: no performance, return or income claims; follow SEC/FINRA marketing rules; include required firm disclosures in the caption
Med spa: show no treatments, before/after or results in this ad; results vary, so no outcome wording; any staff shown in a treatment room must be licensed for what is depicted
Real estate: include brokerage name and license number where the state requires; avoid any wording about who a neighborhood is 'for' (fair housing)
Remove client files, screens and documents from every frame before rendering or filming
